content: Naive set theory is one of the various set theories developed in the study of the foundations of mathematics. It provides an informal framework for understanding mathematical sets, which are commonly encountered in discrete mathematics (e.g., Venn diagrams and Boolean algebra) and are also used in everyday mathematical applications. Sets are fundamental in mathematics, as most mathematical objects, such as numbers, relations, and functions, are defined in terms of sets. Naive set theory serves as an introductory step toward more formal treatments and is sufficient for many purposes. A naive theory is a non-formalized theory that uses natural language to discuss sets. Logical operators like then, not, for some, and for every are not rigorously defined. Studying sets in this informal way at an early stage of mathematics helps develop the ability to work with them. Additionally, understanding set-theoretic concepts from a naive perspective is crucial for grasping the motivation behind the formal axioms of set theory. This article develops a naive theory, where sets are defined informally, and some of their properties are explored. Links to specific axioms of set theory highlight relationships between the informal discussion and formal axiomatization, but not all statements are justified on a formal basis. The first development of set theory was naive set theory, created by Georg Cantor in the late 19th century to enable mathematicians to work consistently with infinite sets. However, the unrestricted assumption that any operation on sets could be performed led to paradoxes, such as Russell's paradox and Berry's paradox. In response, axiomatic set theory was developed to precisely determine which operations were allowed and under what conditions. Today, when mathematicians refer to set theory, they usually mean axiomatic set theory. Informal applications of set theory in other fields are sometimes called naive set theory, but they are generally justifiable within an axiomatic system, typically Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory. Some argue that Cantor's set theory was not inherently implicated in the paradoxes, as he was aware of some of them and did not believe they discredited his theory. However, since Cantor did not provide an axiomatization, this remains uncertain. Frege explicitly axiomatized a theory in which a formalized version of naive set theory could be interpreted, and it was this formal theory that Bertrand Russell addressed when presenting his paradox. These early attempts led to inconsistencies. Naive set theory is not necessarily inconsistent if it correctly specifies the sets allowed to be considered. This can be achieved through definitions, which act as implicit axioms, or by systematically making all axioms explicit, as in Paul Halmos's book Naive Set Theory, which is actually a somewhat informal presentation of the usual axiomatic Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory. It is naive in the sense that the language and notations are those of ordinary informal mathematics, and it does not address the consistency or completeness of the axiom system. In naive set theory, a set is described as a well-defined collection of objects, called elements or members of the set. These objects can be anything, such as numbers, people, or other sets. For example, the number 4 is a member of the set of all even integers. Sets can be finite or infinite. If an object ( x ) is a member of a set ( A ), we say ( x ) belongs to ( A ) or ( x ) is in ( A ), and we write ( x in A ). The symbol ( in ) is derived from the Greek letter epsilon (ε), introduced by Peano in 1888. The symbol ( notin ) is used to denote that ( x notin A ), meaning ( x ) is not in ( A ). Two sets ( A ) and ( B ) are defined to be equal if they have precisely the same elements, meaning every element of ( A ) is an element of ( B ), and every element of ( B ) is an element of ( A ). This is known as the axiom of extensionality. A set is completely determined by its elements, regardless of how it is described. For example, the set with elements 2, 3, and 5 is equal to the set of all prime numbers less than 6. If ( A ) and ( B ) are equal, this is denoted symbolically as ( A = B ). The empty set, often denoted ( emptyset ) or ( {} ), is a set with no members. Since a set is determined entirely by its elements, there can only be one empty set (see the axiom of the empty set). The simplest way to describe a set is to list its elements between curly braces, known as defining a set extensionally. For example, ( {1, 2} ) denotes the set whose only elements are 1 and 2 (see the axiom of pairing). The order of elements is immaterial, so ( {1, 2} = {2, 1} ). Repetition of elements is irrelevant, so ( {1, 2, 2} = {1, 1, 1, 2} = {1, 2} ). This notation can be informally abused by saying something like ( {dogs} ) to indicate the set of all dogs, but mathematicians would usually interpret this as the set containing the single element 'dogs'. An extreme (but correct) example of this notation is ( {} ), which denotes the empty set. We can also use the notation ( {x : P(x)} ), or sometimes ( {x | P(x)} ), to denote the set containing all objects for which the condition ( P ) holds, known as defining a set intensionally. For example, ( {x : x text{ is a real number}} ) denotes the set of real numbers, ( {x : x text{ has blonde hair}} ) denotes the set of everything with blonde hair, and ( {x : x text{ is a dog}} ) denotes the set of all dogs. This notation is called set-builder notation (or set comprehension, particularly in the context of functional programming). Given two sets ( A ) and ( B ), we say that ( A ) is a subset of ( B ) if every element of ( A ) is also an element of ( B ). In particular, ( B ) is a subset of itself; a subset of ( B ) that is not equal to ( B ) is called a proper subset. If ( A ) is a subset of ( B ), we can also say that ( B ) is a superset of ( A ), that ( A ) is contained in ( B ), or that ( B ) contains ( A ). In symbols, ( A subseteq B ) means ( A ) is a subset of ( B ), and ( B supseteq A ) means ( B ) is a superset of ( A ). Some authors use the symbols ( subset ) and ( supset ) for subsets, while others use these symbols only for proper subsets. For clarity, one can explicitly use the symbols ( subsetneq ) and ( supsetneq ) to indicate non-equality. In this encyclopedia, ( subseteq ) and ( supseteq ) are used for subsets, while ( subset ) and ( supset ) are reserved for proper subsets. The set of all subsets of a given set ( A ) is called the power set of ( A ) and is denoted by ( 2^A ) or ( P(A) ). If the set ( A ) has ( n ) elements, then ( P(A) ) will have ( 2^n ) elements. In certain contexts, we may consider all sets under consideration as being subsets of some given universal set. For example, if we are investigating properties of the real numbers ( mathbb{R} ) (and subsets of ( mathbb{R} )), we may take ( mathbb{R} ) as our universal set. A universal set is only temporarily defined by the context; there is no such thing as a universal universal set, the set of everything (see paradoxes below). Given a universal set ( U ) and a subset ( A ) of ( U ), we may define the complement of ( A ) (in ( U )) as the set of all members of ( U ) which are not members of ( A ). This is denoted as ( A^C ) or sometimes ( A' ). For example, if ( mathbb{Z} ) is the universal set, then the complement of the set of odd integers is the set of even integers. Given two sets ( A ) and ( B ), their union is the set consisting of all objects which are elements of ( A ), ( B ), or both. It is denoted by ( A cup B ). The intersection of ( A ) and ( B ) is the set of all objects which are both in ( A ) and ( B ). It is denoted by ( A cap B ). The relative complement of ( B ) relative to ( A ), also known as the set-theoretic difference of ( A ) and ( B ), is the set of all objects that belong to ( A ) but not to ( B ). It is written as ( A setminus B ) or ( A B ). An ordered pair is a collection of two objects where one can be distinguished as the first element and the other as the second element. Formally, an ordered pair ( (a, b) ) is defined as the set ( {{a}, {a, b}} ). Two ordered pairs ( (a, b) ) and ( (c, d) ) are equal if and only if ( a = c ) and ( b = d ). The Cartesian product of two sets ( A ) and ( B ), denoted ( A times B ), is the set of all ordered pairs ( (a, b) ) where ( a in A ) and ( b in B ). This concept can be extended to ordered triples, quadruples, and so on. Finally, naive set theory encounters paradoxes, such as Russell's paradox, which arise from the unrestricted formation of sets. Axiomatic set theory resolves these issues by placing restrictions on the types of sets that can be formed.
